question: A department has used Claude to redraft a board paper over six rounds. Each round was reviewed by whoever was free that week, and each reviewer applied their own idea of what a good board paper looks like. What is the greatest risk?
options: A) No shared standard of quality, so the team cannot tell whether the paper improved
B) The reviewers may use up their monthly usage allowance before the sixth round ends
C) Claude may carry wording the reviewers rejected in earlier rounds into later drafts
D) The paper may end up shorter than the format the board has asked for in the past
correct_answers: A) No shared standard of quality, so the team cannot tell whether the paper improved
explanations: Correct. Six reviewers applying six private ideas of quality means each round pulls the draft in a different direction, so the department has no agreed measure against which to judge round six versus round one. Anthropic's AI Fluency material defines Product Discernment as evaluating the quality of what the model produces for accuracy, appropriateness, coherence and relevance, and describes Discernment as working hand-in-hand with Description in a continuous feedback loop; that loop only converges when the criteria being applied stay the same from round to round.

Usage allowance caps how much work can be sent to Claude in a period, and reviewers would notice they were running low well before it halted the cycle. It says nothing about whether the drafting process is producing a better board paper.

Wording from an earlier round can resurface when every round shares the same conversation, but a reviewer reading the draft will see it and ask for it to go. It does not explain why the department cannot tell whether the paper is getting better.

A draft drifting away from the length the board is used to is visible on the page and corrected with one more instruction. It is a symptom of an unmanaged review cycle rather than the thing that makes six rounds of work impossible to evaluate.
